# Algeria TRAVEL SURVIVAL KIT **Traveler Types Covered**: Budget/Luxury/Family/Solo ## 1. SIM CARD SOLUTIONS **Purpose**: Obtain local mobile connectivity for calls, data, and internet access. | **Aspect** | **Details to Find (Algeria)** | | :-------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Providers** | Ooredoo, Mobilis, Djezzy | | **Price Options** | - **Ooredoo:** 1000 DZD (5GB/7 days), 2000 DZD (15GB/15 days), 3000 DZD (30GB/30 days)
- **Mobilis:** 900 DZD (4GB/7 days), 1800 DZD (12GB/15 days), 2800 DZD (25GB/30 days)
- **Djezzy:** 950 DZD (4.5GB/7 days), 1900 DZD (13GB/15 days), 2900 DZD (28GB/30 days) | | **Data Allocation** | Plans typically offer high-speed 4G data, then throttle to 128 kbps. | | **Validity Period** | From 7 days to 30 days depending on the package. | | **Hotspot/Tethering** | Generally allowed on most plans. | | **Coverage** | Good coverage in major cities (Algiers, Oran, Constantine) and coastal regions. Inland and Saharan areas can be spotty. | | **Where to Buy** | Airport (Houari Boumediene ALG), official telecom shops in major cities, large convenience stores. Bring passport for registration. | | **Alternative: eSIM** | Airalo, Holafly offer regional eSIMs for North Africa starting from ~$9-15 USD for 1GB/7 days. | #### Recommendations Framework - **Short trips (3-5 days) + visiting neighboring countries?** → Physical SIM from airport for immediate local number; eSIM for regional data if connectivity is poor. - **Staying 1-4 weeks?** → Longer validity plans with highest data allocation from official provider shops for better support. - **Digital nomad preferences?** → eSIM for convenience or a high-data physical SIM from Ooredoo/Mobilis. - **Budget-conscious?** → Compare per-GB cost, Mobilis often offers competitive rates. --- ## 2. AIRPORT TRANSFERS **Purpose**: Navigate from main airport to nearest major city center efficiently. **Route**: From Houari Boumediene Airport (ALG) to Algiers City Center | **Mode** | **Duration (approx.)** | **Cost (DZD)** | **Booking** | **Convenience** | **Best For** | | :--------------------------- | :--------------------- | :----------------- | :----------------------------- | :-------------- | :------------------------- | | **Airport Bus (ETUSA)** | 45-60 minutes | 50 DZD | Ticket on board | Good | Budget travelers, daytime | | **Ride-hailing (Yassir/Careem)** | 30-45 minutes | 800-1500 DZD | App-based | Very Good | Door-to-door, late night | | **Taxi (Licensed)** | 30-45 minutes | 1000-2000 DZD | Airport counter/outside | Good | Groups, luggage, comfort | | **Hotel Shuttle** | Varies | 2000-3500 DZD | Contact hotel in advance | Excellent | Pre-arranged, convenience | | **Car Rental** | Flexible | 4000-8000 DZD/day | Online agencies/airport desks | Excellent | Multiple days, exploration | #### Detail Each Option With - **Airport Bus (ETUSA)**: Boarding at Terminal 1 exit. Frequency every 30-60 minutes. Final drop-off at Tafourah/Grande Poste in city center. Purchase ticket on bus. Operates 5:00 AM - 9:00 PM. - **Ride-hailing (Yassir/Careem)**: Pick-up point usually clearly marked outside arrivals. Requires local SIM/eSIM for app use. Upfront pricing, driver tracking. Available 24/7. Time estimates vary heavily with Algiers traffic. - **Taxi (Licensed)**: Official taxi stand directly outside arrivals. Agree on fare *before* starting the journey. Often white or yellow. Available 24/7. Expect surcharges for late night. - **Hotel Shuttle**: Pre-arranged through your hotel. Confirm exact pick-up instructions with the hotel. - **Car Rental**: Desks for international and local agencies (e.g., Avis, Europcar, Rent-a-Car Algeria) are inside the arrivals hall. --- ## 3. CURRENCY EXCHANGE **Purpose**: Convert home currency to local currency at best rates. **Current Exchange Rate (approx. at time of writing)**: 1 USD = ~135-138 Algerian Dinar (DZD) in official markets. Black market rates can be significantly higher (1 USD = ~200-220 DZD), but are illegal and risky. #### Best Exchange Locations | **Location** | **Why It's Best** | **Address (Example)** | **Hours** | **Rates (vs. USD)** | **Tips** | | :------------------ | :-------------------------------- | :-------------------- | :------------------ | :------------------ | :-------------------------------------------- | | **Banks** | Official, secure, transparent | BNP Paribas (Algiers) | Mon-Fri 8:30AM-3:30PM | Official rate | Bring passport, expect queues, exchange major currencies (USD, EUR, GBP). | | **Post Offices** | Government-backed, reliable | Grande Poste (Algiers)| Mon-Thu 8AM-5PM, Sat 8AM-1PM | Official rate | Limited foreign currency services, but an option. | | **Hotels (Major)** | Convenient, accessible | Hotel El Aurassi | 24/7 (lobby) | Slightly worse than banks | Good for small emergency exchanges outside bank hours. | #### Alternative Methods | **Method** | **Pros** | **Cons** | **Best For** | | :------------------- | :------------------------------- | :------------------------------- | :------------------------ | | **ATM Withdrawal** | Mid-market rates, convenient | Bank fees (local + home), daily withdrawal limits, DZD often scarce. | Reliable, steady cash needs (if ATMs work). | | **Airport Exchange** | Immediate access | Higher margins, worse rates than city banks. | Emergency only on arrival. | | **Credit Card** | Tracking, secure, often best rates if no FTT. | Foreign transaction fees, not widely accepted outside major hotels/stores. | Large purchases in modern establishments. | #### Universal Tips - Avoid exchanging at airport unless absolutely necessary (rates are generally 5-10% worse). - Compare rates between 2-3 official money changers or banks. - Carry cash in smaller denominations for day-to-day purchases. - Always check for hidden commissions before exchanging. - Have small cash on arrival for immediate needs (taxi, tips). - Be aware of the unofficial "black market" for currency exchange, especially for Euros, but exercise extreme caution due to legality and safety risks. Stick to official channels. --- ## 4. MUST-TRY FOODS **Purpose**: Experience authentic local cuisine and signature dishes. 🍽️ **Couscous (كسكس)** – Main Course → What: Steamed semolina served with a rich stew of vegetables (carrots, zucchini, chickpeas) and often meat (lamb, chicken, or beef). The national dish. → Where: Almost any traditional restaurant (e.g., Restaurant El Djenina in Algiers) or local homes. → Price: 800-1500 DZD → Try with: A glass of leben (fermented buttermilk) or mint tea. 🍽️ **Chorba Frik (شربة فريك)** – Soup → What: A hearty, flavorful tomato-based soup with green wheat (frik), vegetables, and often lamb or chicken. A staple during Ramadan. → Where: Popular in local eateries, especially during winter or Ramadan. → Price: 300-600 DZD → Try with: Fresh lemon wedges and bourek (fried pastry rolls). 🍽️ **Tagine (طاجين)** – Main Course → What: Slow-cooked savory stew named after the earthenware pot it's cooked in. Varieties include chicken with olives and preserved lemon, or lamb with prunes and almonds. → Where: Traditional Algerian restaurants. → Price: 1200-2500 DZD → Try with: Freshly baked bread to scoop up the sauce. 🍽️ **Mhadjeb (محاجب)** – Street Snack → What: Thin, savory semolina crepes filled with a spicy tomato and onion mixture, then folded and grilled until crispy. → Where: Street food stalls and small eateries across cities. → Price: 100-200 DZD per piece → Try with: Harissa (chilli paste) for an extra kick. 🍽️ **Griwesh (قريوش)** – Dessert → What: A fried, intricate pastry shaped like a flower, drizzled with honey and often sprinkled with sesame seeds. → Where: Bakeries (Pâtisserie La Ruche), local markets, and sweet shops. → Price: 50-150 DZD per piece → Try with: Strong Algerian coffee or sweet mint tea. 🍽️ **Mint Tea (الشاي بالنعناع)** – Beverage → What: Sweet green tea infused with fresh mint leaves, often served in small glasses with elaborate pouring. A symbol of hospitality. → Where: Offered everywhere – homes, cafes, restaurants. → Price: 100-250 DZD per pot/glass → Try with: Any meal or as a refreshing break. 🍽️ **Makroud (مقروض)** – Dessert → What: Semolina cookies filled with date paste, deep-fried or baked, and then soaked in honey or syrup. → Where: Pâtisseries, traditional sweet shops, and local markets. → Price: 50-100 DZD per piece → Try with: A cup of traditional Arabic coffee. --- ## 6. UNIQUE & BRANDED ITEMS TO BUY **Purpose**: Purchase country-specific products worth bringing home. | **Item** | **Why Worth Buying** | **Where to Buy** | **Price Range (DZD / USD)** | **Packaging Tips** | | :------------------ | :--------------------------------- | :---------------------------------- | :-------------------------- | :---------------------------------------- | | **Dates (Deglet Noor)** | World-renowned, sweet, nutritious, high quality. | Central markets, specialized date shops, supermarkets (Ardis). | 300-1500 DZD/kg (~$2-11 USD) | Airtight containers, away from heat. | | **Berber Jewelry** | Handcrafted, unique silver designs, cultural significance. | Artisan markets (e.g., in Tizi Ouzou), specialty shops in Algiers. | 3000-20000+ DZD (~$22-150+ USD) | Protect from scratching, wrap individually. | | **Traditional Pottery** | Hand-painted tagines, bowls, decorative items; vibrant colors. | Souk (markets), artisan workshops, craft stores. | 500-5000 DZD (~$4-37 USD) | Bubble wrap, sturdy box, carry-on if possible. | | **Spices** | High quality, aromatic (Ras el Hanout, cumin, paprika, saffron). | Spice vendors in local markets (e.g., Bab El Oued market). | 100-500 DZD/100g (~$1-4 USD) | Airtight bags/jars to preserve aroma. | | **Leather Goods** | Handcrafted bags, wallets, belts; good value. | Artisanal shops, leather markets. | 2000-10000 DZD (~$15-75 USD) | Stuff with paper to maintain shape. | | **Algerian Coffee** | Locally roasted blends, rich and strong. | Supermarkets, local grocery stores. | 300-800 DZD/500g (~$2-6 USD) | Vacuum-sealed bags for freshness. | | **Traditional Textiles** | Hand-woven rugs (e.g., from Ghardaia), embroidered fabrics. | Artisan markets, specialized carpet shops. | 5000-50000+ DZD (~$37-370+ USD) | Roll or fold carefully, protect from moisture. | --- ## 7. SUPERMARKETS & CONVENIENCE STORES **Purpose**: Access everyday items, snacks, and groceries reliably. **Ardis (أرديس)** - **Best for**: Full grocery shopping, household items, some imported goods. - **Specialty**: Largest hypermarket chain, wide selection, often includes mall-like shopping. - **Hours**: 9:00 AM - 10:00 PM daily. - **Locations**: Major cities like Algiers (Mohammadia, Hydra), Oran. Closest to tourist areas: Ardis Mohammadia, easily accessible by taxi. **Uno (أونو)** - **Best for**: Mid-range grocery shopping, fresh produce, meat, and dairy. - **Specialty**: Good balance of local and some international brands. - **Hours**: 8:30 AM - 9:00 PM daily. - **Locations**: Several branches in Algiers and other major cities. **Point Chaud (بوان شو)** - **Best for**: Convenience items, snacks, drinks, basic toiletries, quick meals. - **Specialty**: Small format grocery/convenience store, typically open longer hours. - **Hours**: 7:00 AM - 11:00 PM daily. - **Locations**: Numerous locations in urban areas, often found in residential and commercial districts. **Pharmacies (Pharmacie)** - **Best for**: Over-the-counter medication, first-aid supplies, personal care, some cosmetics. - **Specialty**: Highly regulated, professional advice available. Look for the green cross sign. - **Hours**: Typically 8:00 AM - 8:00 PM, with rotating night-duty pharmacies. - **Locations**: Ubiquitous in all towns and cities. --- ## 8. MARKETS (Day & Night) **Purpose**: Experience local culture, find deals, and enjoy street food. #### Night Markets (Less common in traditional sense, more extended day markets) | **Market Name** | **Location** | **Open Hours** | **Best For** | **What to Expect** | **Pro Tips** | | :-------------------- | :----------------------- | :---------------- | :---------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- | | **Port Said Square Market (Algiers)** | Rue Larbi Ben M'hidi | Daily, until ~8:00 PM | Handicrafts, books, souvenirs, street snacks. | Bustling square with vendors selling various goods, lively atmosphere. | Bargain respectfully, watch for pickpockets in crowded areas. | #### Day Markets | **Market Name** | **Location** | **Open Hours** | **Best For** | **What to Expect** | **Pro Tips** | | :---------------------- | :--------------------------- | :------------------ | :------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------- | | **Bab El Oued Market (Algiers)** | Bab El Oued district | Daily, 8:00 AM - 6:00 PM | Fresh produce, spices, meat, household goods. | Authentic local market experience, vibrant and busy. | Go early for best selection, practice your French/Arabic. | | **Place des Martyrs Souk (Algiers)** | Near Ketchaoua Mosque | Daily, 9:00 AM - 7:00 PM | Local crafts, textiles, jewelry, souvenirs. | Smaller, more tourist-friendly market with traditional goods. | Good place to find quality souvenirs, compare prices. | #### Universal Night/Day Market Tips - Carry cash (small denominations) as most stalls don't accept cards. - Visit early to beat crowds and for the freshest produce. - Bargaining is expected in most markets; do so politely and with a smile. - Food stalls often offer the freshest and most authentic local snacks. - Best for photography and atmosphere, especially during cooler parts of the day. --- ## 9. BEST ALCOHOLIC DRINKS **Purpose**: Try region-specific beverages and understand drinking culture. #### Local Beers | **Brand** | **Type** | **Flavor Profile** | **Where to Buy** | **Price (DZD)** | **Try At** | | :-------- | :----------- | :---------------------- | :--------------------- | :-------------- | :-------------------- | | **Tango** | Lager | Light, crisp, refreshing| Licensed supermarkets, hotel bars. | 150-300 | Hotel bars, private clubs. | | **Flag** | Lager | Milder, standard lager | Licensed supermarkets, hotel bars. | 150-300 | Licensed restaurants. | #### Spirits & Liqueurs | **Drink** | **Type** | **Origin** | **Taste** | **Where to Buy** | **Price (DZD)** | | :-------- | :--------- | :--------------- | :-------------------- | :----------------- | :-------------- | | **Boukha**| Fig Brandy | Tunisia (regional)| Fruity, strong, unique| Specialty liquor stores, some duty-free. | 1500-3000 | Limited availability. | #### Wine & Rice Wine - Algeria has a history of wine production, though it's less prominent now. - Local wines, primarily reds and rosés, are available, often dry and robust. - Traditional rice wines are not a feature of Algerian culture. #### Where to Buy | **Outlet Type** | **Best For** | **Price Level** | **Selection** | | :------------------------ | :------------------------------------------ | :-------------- | :------------ | | **Convenience stores** | Very limited to non-alcoholic beverages. | N/A | None | | **Supermarkets (licensed sections)** | Variety of local beers and wines. | Mid-range | Good | | **Specialty liquor stores** | Broader selection of spirits, imported alcohol. | High | Excellent | | **Duty-free (at airport)**| Deals on international brands. | Discount | Large | #### Drinking Culture Tips - **Legal drinking age**: 18. - **Where alcohol is sold**: Alcohol sales are restricted. It's primarily available in licensed hotels, a few dedicated restaurants in major cities, and specific liquor stores (often with discreet signage). Supermarkets may have a separate, often less visible, section. - **Social drinking etiquette**: Public consumption of alcohol is generally frowned upon and can be illegal. Drink discreetly in licensed premises. Respect local customs; Algeria is a Muslim-majority country. - **Tipping customs in bars**: Tipping is appreciated but not mandatory, generally 10% is sufficient. - **Peak drinking hours**: Evenings, primarily in hotel bars or private settings. --- ## 10. BEST PUBS & BARS **Purpose**: Find quality nightlife venues for evening entertainment. #### Selection Criteria (Algeria) - Due to local customs, most venues are found within international hotels or are discrete establishments. - Ambiance tends to be more relaxed and upscale rather than boisterous club scenes. **SkyBar (at Hotel El Aurassi)** - **Vibe**: Upscale, panoramic views of Algiers Bay, relaxed lounge atmosphere. - **Location**: Avenue Frantz Fanon, Algiers (Hotel El Aurassi). - **Hours**: 6:00 PM - 1:00 AM. - **Specialties**: Classic cocktails, premium spirits, international wine list, light bites. - **Pro Tips**: Dress smart-casual. Best for sunset views. Reservations recommended on weekends. **The Irish Pub (at Hotel Mercure Algiers)** - **Vibe**: Cozy, familiar pub atmosphere, often with live music or sports screenings. - **Location**: Route de l'Université, Bab Ezzouar, Algiers (Hotel Mercure). - **Hours**: 5:00 PM - Midnight. - **Specialties**: Local and international beers, pub food menu. - **Pro Tips**: Popular with expats and business travelers. Good for a relaxed evening. **La Brasserie (at Hotel Sofitel Algiers Hamma Garden)** - **Vibe**: Elegant, sophisticated, often with a jazz or soft music background. - **Location**: 172 Rue Hassiba Ben Bouali, Hamma, Algiers (Hotel Sofitel). - **Hours**: 6:00 PM - 1:00 AM. - **Specialties**: Fine wines, spirits, cocktails, and a French-inspired food menu. - **Pro Tips**: More of a restaurant-bar feel, excellent for a quiet, refined drink. **El Boustan (at Hotel Marriott Algiers)** - **Vibe**: Modern, spacious lounge bar, often hosting events or DJ nights. - **Location**: Centre Commercial et de Loisirs de Bab Ezzouar, Algiers (Hotel Marriott). - **Hours**: 5:00 PM - 2:00 AM. - **Specialties**: Wide selection of international drinks, contemporary setting. - **Pro Tips**: Good for larger groups or a livelier (by Algerian standards) evening out. --- ## BONUS SECTIONS - Local Festivals & Events Algeria hosts various cultural and religious festivals. Look out for local music festivals, especially during summer in coastal cities, and traditional celebrations like Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. The Timgad International Festival is a prominent annual music event. ### 11. LOCAL CUSTOMS & ETIQUETTE #### 11a. Temple & Sacred Site Dress Code Conservative dress is essential when visiting mosques and religious sites in Algeria. Always verify specific rules, but general guidelines apply. | **Rule** | **What to Check** | **Enforcement Level** | | :---------------------- | :------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------ | | **Shoulders covered** | Sleeveless tops / tank tops prohibited | Strict at mosques. | | **Knees covered** | Shorts / mini-skirts prohibited | Strictly enforced at mosques. | | **Footwear** | Shoes removed before entry | Mandatory at mosques. | | **Head covering** | Required for women at mosques | Mandatory for women at mosques. | | **Colour restrictions** | None generally, but modest colors are preferred. | Not typically enforced. | | **Sarong/Wrap rental** | Not typically available. | Not common. | > **Pro format tip:** Always state: _"T-shirts and lightweight long pants are the perfect temple outfit — simple, cool, and always accepted."_ > > In Algeria, loose-fitting long pants or skirts, and long-sleeved tops are ideal for visiting mosques. Women should carry a headscarf to cover their hair before entering. #### 11b. The Head, Feet & Body — Cultural Hierarchy Algerian culture, like many Islamic societies, places importance on body parts in social interactions. | **Universal Rule** | **Algeria-Specific Guidance** | | :------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **The head is sacred** | Avoid touching an adult's head without permission. Less strict for children but still polite to avoid. | | **The feet are considered low/impure** | Never point the soles of your feet at a person, especially an elder, or a religious object. When sitting, tuck feet away. | | **Passing objects** | Use the right hand for passing objects, food, or money. Using the left hand (considered unclean) is impolite. | #### 11c. Monk Interactions & Religious Etiquette In a Muslim-majority country like Algeria, interactions with Imams (religious leaders) and during prayer times require respectful behavior. | **Rule** | **Detail** | **Who It Applies To** | | :------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------- | | **Women cannot touch religious leaders** | No physical contact, particularly with Imams in religious settings. | All women. | | **Women handing items to religious leaders** | Place item on a surface or table if direct contact is culturally sensitive. | All women. | | **Men offering items** | Can be handed directly, using the right hand respectfully. | All men. | | **Photography during prayer** | Always avoid photographing people during prayer. Ask permission otherwise. | All visitors. | | **Entering mosque grounds** | Dress code applies; remove shoes before entering prayer halls. | All visitors. | | **Observing Ramadan/prayer times** | Be mindful of prayer calls (Adhan) and respect those fasting during Ramadan. | All visitors. | #### 11d. Saving Face & Conflict Resolution "Saving face" is crucial in Algerian social interactions, emphasizing respect and avoiding public embarrassment. | **Key Rule** | **Algeria-Specific Guidance** | | :------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Never raise your voice/show anger** | Maintain a calm and polite demeanor; public outbursts are very poorly received. | | **Smile through difficult negotiations** | Politeness and patience, often accompanied by a smile, are effective when bargaining. | | **Public confrontations always backfire** | Address any issues privately and quietly to ensure a better chance of resolution. | | **"Yes" does not always mean yes** | Sometimes a vague answer or change of subject may imply refusal without direct "no." | | **Patience is a virtue** | Remaining calm and persistent is crucial, especially in bureaucratic or market interactions. | #### 11e. Responsible Tourism & Child Welfare Supporting responsible tourism and protecting child welfare is vital in Algeria. | **Core Principle** | **Algeria-Specific Guidance** | | :------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Do not give money/gifts to begging children.** | This perpetuates cycles of poverty and keeps children out of school. | | **Support legitimate alternatives instead.** | Seek out established charities, cultural centers, or fair-trade shops. | | **Orphanage tourism is harmful.** | Avoid visiting or donating to orphanages; they can exploit children. | | **Animal welfare.** | Do not participate in activities that exploit animals. | | **Ask before photographing people.** | Always politely ask for permission, especially for women and children. | #### 11f. General Social Customs & Greetings Understanding general social customs will enhance your experience in Algeria. | **Custom** | **Algeria-Specific Practice** | | :--------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Greeting style** | Handshakes are common between same-sex individuals. Men may exchange kisses on cheeks. Women may air kiss. | | **Tipping culture** | Optional but appreciated in restaurants (5-10%), for taxi drivers (round up), hotel staff. | | **Dress outside temples** | Modest dress is generally expected, especially for women, to respect local sensibilities. | | **Photography restrictions** | Avoid photographing military installations, police, or sensitive government buildings. | | **Public displays of affection** | Keep public displays of affection minimal or avoid them, especially between unmarried couples. | | **Bargaining norms** | Expected in souks (markets) and with informal taxis; less so in modern shops/restaurants. | | **Dining etiquette** | Often involves communal dishes; use your right hand. Wait for the host to indicate when to start eating. | ### 12. SAFETY & PRACTICAL INFORMATION #### 12a. Vaccinations & Preventative Health Consult a medical professional well before your trip for personalized vaccination advice. | **Vaccine / Medication** | **Priority Level** | **Notes** | | :--------------------------------- | :------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Hepatitis A** | Strongly recommended | Transmitted through contaminated food/water — essential for any developing country | | **Hepatitis B** | Recommended | Especially for longer stays or those in medical/healthcare settings | | **Typhoid** | Recommended | High risk in areas with poor sanitation and street food consumption | | **Tetanus / Diphtheria (Td/Tdap)** | Recommended | Ensure booster is current (within 10 years) | | **Rabies pre-exposure** | Destination-specific | Recommended for adventurous travel or areas with limited post-exposure treatment. | | **Malaria prophylaxis** | Generally NOT needed | Not typically required for major cities or coastal Algeria. Consult a travel doctor for specific remote areas. | #### 12b. Mosquito-Borne Illness & Insect Protection Mosquito-borne diseases can be a concern, especially in rural areas or during warmer months. | **Disease** | **Mosquito Type** | **Peak Risk** | **Prevention** | | :--------------- | :----------------------- | :-------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- | | **West Nile Virus** | Culex (night biting) | Summer, early autumn | DEET repellent, covered clothing, mosquito nets. | | **Leishmaniasis**| Sandflies (dusk/dawn) | Rural areas, year-round | DEET repellent, covered clothing, avoid going out at dusk/dawn. | #### 12c. Water & Food Safety Strict adherence to water and food safety guidelines is crucial to prevent illness. | **Source** | **Safety** | **Guidance** | | :-------------------------- | :----------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Tap water** | Unsafe | Do NOT drink tap water in Algeria. | | **Sealed bottled water** | Safe | Standard recommendation; widely available and affordable. | | **Ice in restaurants** | Varies | In tourist restaurants: usually safe. In local eateries: confirm it's from filtered water or avoid. | | **Filtered water stations** | Safe | Available at many hotels; refill personal bottles. | | **Boiled water** | Safe | Reliable if fully boiled. | #### 12d. Personal Safety & Crime Awareness Overall safety rating: Moderate risk for tourists. Violent crime against tourists is rare, but petty crime is common in urban areas. Political stability has improved, but remain vigilant. **ISSUE: Petty Theft & Pickpocketing** WHERE IT HAPPENS: Crowded markets (souks), public transport (buses, trams), major tourist attractions, and busy city centers like Algiers' Place des Martyrs. HOW IT HAPPENS: Opportunistic thieves target distracted individuals. Bags can be unzipped, wallets lifted from pockets, and phones snatched from tables. HOW TO AVOID IT: Keep valuables out of sight and secure. Use a cross-body bag worn to the front or a money belt under clothing. Avoid displaying expensive electronics or jewelry. Be especially aware in dense crowds. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Report immediately to the local police (Sûreté Nationale) and obtain a police report for insurance claims. Contact your embassy for assistance. **ISSUE: Bag-snatching** WHERE IT HAPPENS: Primarily in busy urban areas, particularly from pedestrians near roads or from café terraces. HOW IT HAPPENS: Individuals on motorbikes or on foot can quickly snatch bags, especially those worn loosely or placed on chairs. HOW TO AVOID IT: Wear bags securely across your body, not just over one shoulder. If dining outdoors, keep bags on your lap or between your feet, not on an adjacent chair. Be aware of your surroundings, especially when walking near traffic. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Do not resist if someone tries to snatch your bag; prioritize your physical safety. Report to police and embassy. **ISSUE: Taxi Overcharging / Scams** WHERE IT HAPPENS: Airports, bus stations, major hotel areas, and popular tourist sites. HOW IT HAPPENS: Unlicensed taxis or drivers may quote exorbitant fares, claim meters are broken, or take longer routes. HOW TO AVOID IT: Use licensed taxis if possible, and always agree on a price *before* starting the journey. Alternatively, use ride-hailing apps like Yassir or Careem for transparent pricing. Have small denominations ready to avoid claims of no change. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: If a dispute arises, remain firm but polite. Note the taxi number or license plate. If you feel unsafe, exit the taxi at a safe, public location. **ISSUE: "Fake Guide" / Tourist Assistance Scams** WHERE IT HAPPENS: Near major historical sites, museums, and busy squares. HOW IT HAPPENS: Individuals may approach tourists offering unsolicited "help," directions, or "official" guide services, then demand inflated fees or lead tourists to overpriced shops. HOW TO AVOID IT: Politely decline any unsolicited offers of assistance. If you need a guide, arrange one through your hotel or a reputable tour company. Be skeptical of anyone who seems overly friendly or insistent. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Firmly state you are not interested and walk away. If pressured, seek out uniformed officials or enter a nearby established business. **ISSUE: Road Safety (Driving & Pedestrians)** WHERE IT HAPPENS: Throughout the country, especially in congested urban areas and on rural roads. HOW IT HAPPENS: Aggressive driving, poor road conditions, and disregard for traffic laws are common. Pedestrians often cross roads without looking. HOW TO AVOID IT: Exercise extreme caution as a pedestrian; assume drivers may not yield. If driving, be defensive, avoid night driving on unlit roads, and be prepared for unexpected obstacles (animals, poor signage). Public transport or ride-hailing is often a safer alternative. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: If involved in an accident, contact police immediately. If witnessing one, offer assistance if safe, but prioritize your own safety. **High-risk areas**: Areas bordering Mali, Niger, and Libya, as well as parts of the Sahara, are considered high-risk due to security concerns (terrorism, kidnapping). Avoid these regions entirely unless on an organized tour with expert security. **Safe areas**: Major cities like Algiers, Oran, and Constantine, and the well-traveled coastal routes are generally safe for tourists, especially during the day. **Night safety**: Exercise increased vigilance after dark, especially in unlit areas or isolated streets. Stick to well-populated and well-lit areas. Take licensed taxis or ride-hailing apps instead of walking alone. **Local laws**: Be aware that Algerian laws reflect Islamic traditions. Public consumption of alcohol is forbidden. Possession or trafficking of drugs carries severe penalties. #### 12e. SEASONAL CONSIDERATIONS Algeria experiences a Mediterranean climate along the coast (hot, dry summers; mild, wet winters) and an arid desert climate inland. Summers (June-August) can be extremely hot, especially in the south. Spring (March-May) and autumn (September-November) offer the most pleasant weather for travel. ### 14. GENERAL TIPS Consider purchasing a local tourist SIM upon arrival. ATMs can be unreliable, so carry sufficient cash. Bargaining is common in markets. Power sockets are Type C and F, 230V with a frequency of 50Hz, so bring a universal adapter. Free Wi-Fi is available in most hotels and some cafes.
